doctrine:
SCIENTIFIC ADVERTISING · Claude C. Hopkins · Dense Operating Doctrine

1. ADVERTISING = SALESMANSHIP IN PRINT (Ch 2). The ONLY purpose of an ad is to make sales. It is not for brand awareness, not for entertainment, not to keep a name visible. Judge every element the way you judge a salesman: does it sell? If a salesman would not do it, do not do it in print. Fine writing is a liability. Humor is a liability. Loud type is a liability. Address one typical buyer face-to-face, not the mass.

2. MAIL ORDER IS THE COURT OF TRUTH (Ch 4). Mail order advertising reveals every lie. Cost per reply and cost per customer are the only metrics that matter. Every principle Hopkins teaches was proved by mail order returns first. Rules derived: small type pays as well as large; borders waste space; every inch must earn; no decorative pictures; no entertainment; tell the complete story; 'the more you tell the more you sell.' Any ad that cannot survive mail order scrutiny is not a good ad.

3. THE HEADLINE IS HALF THE AD (Ch 5). The headline selects the reader. A bad headline on a great ad = zero returns. Hopkins spent more time on headlines than on body copy. A headline change alone multiplied returns 5x to 10x on the same ad. Rule: a headline must hail only the people you want, not everyone. Clever or blind headlines attract the wrong crowd and miss the right one. Run multiple headline tests on every significant product.

4. PSYCHOLOGY RULES (Ch 6). Key psychology levers Hopkins proved by test: (a) Curiosity is the strongest human incentive — use it. (b) Cheapness repels; people want to feel they can afford the best. Price signals quality. (c) Pay-later outperforms try-and-return-for-refund: the horse story (come pay me then vs come back for your money). (d) Personalization creates ownership psychology — name in gilt on a book drove hundreds of thousands of sales. (e) Exclusivity appeals to identity: 'offer limited to executives' outperforms the same offer to all. (f) Positive always out-pulls negative four to one. Show the beautiful result, not the problem you cure.

5. BE SPECIFIC; GENERALITIES HAVE ZERO WEIGHT (Ch 7). 'Best in the world' is worthless. '9 percent net profit, here is the actual cost breakdown' wins. 'Softens the beard in one minute. Maintains creamy fullness for 10 minutes. Result of 130 tested formulas.' That specific shaving soap destroyed a saturated market. One brewer described his plate-glass cooling room, four-times-washed bottles, 4,000-foot wells, 1,018 experiments for yeast — all things every brewer did, but no one had stated. He dominated beer advertising. Specific = believable. Vague = discounted.

6. TELL THE FULL STORY IN ONE AD (Ch 8). Readers do not return for part two. Serial ads almost never connect. You have one shot. Bring every relevant argument in that single exposure. Brevity is not a virtue if it omits a claim that would have converted 20 percent of readers. Long copy beats short copy when the space is well-used, not padded.

7. ART/PICTURES MUST EARN THEIR SPACE (Ch 9). Every picture is expensive. Use pictures only when they sell better than the same space in type. No decorative pictures. No eccentric pictures — they damage credibility and pull attention from the headline. Color rarely pays better than black-and-white (with exception of food/product shots where color approximates exhibition). Repeated pictures are fine — readers you want are new readers who have not seen them.

8. DO NOT TRY TO CHANGE HABITS; RIDE EXISTING DESIRES (Ch 10). Changing habits is prohibitively expensive. Educating consumers to use a product category for the first time is a charity that benefits rivals. Instead: find the desire that already exists, satisfy it. The dentifrice maker who tried to educate people on tooth-brushing failed; the one who went to already-converted people and offered a beauty/cosmetic appeal won. Watch for emerging trends — enter when desire is already being created by others.

9. RESEARCH BEFORE YOU WRITE (Ch 11). Hopkins read entire medical libraries to find one scientific fact that became the Puffed Wheat campaign. He read volumes to find a single caffeine fact that repositioned decaffeinated coffee. 130 interviewers canvassed consumers on food preferences. 12,000 physicians surveyed. 1,000 men surveyed on shaving desires. The pork-and-beans canvass found 96 percent baked beans at home; the winning campaign was not about brand but about switching from home-baked — a discovery that only research revealed.

10. STRATEGY: OWN THE GENERIC NAME OR LOSE THE HARVEST (Ch 12). Pioneers who use a descriptive name (Toasted Corn Flakes, Malted Milk, Horlick's) build demand for the category and then watch competitors take the crop. Coined, ownable names (Kodak, Vaseline, Jell-O, Postum) let the builder own the demand they create. This is a founding decision that cannot be corrected later. Vaseline nearly monopolized petroleum jelly because the name was coined. Toasted Corn Flakes built a category Kellogg's then dominated.

11. SAMPLES MUST BE EARNED, NOT SCATTERED (Ch 13). Samples distributed to uninterested people are wasted and cheapen the product. The right method: create desire and a mental impression first through the ad, then give the sample only to people who demonstrate interest by some effort (mailing a coupon, presenting it at a store). The sample then confirms expectations already set. Requesting a sample by mail costs 70 cents each; by store coupon presentation 18-22 cents. Make response as friction-free as possible (store pickup is better than postage-required mail). Never charge for a sample — the cost of the dime or stamp far exceeds the price in lost responses.

12. DISTRIBUTION STRATEGY (Ch 14). Local first, then national. Use sample coupons to force dealer stocking — no dealer lets coupon-bearing customers walk to a competitor. Send dealers advance proof of upcoming coupon ads listing their store; they will pre-stock to capture those sales. Palmolive and Puffed Grains built national distribution this way in one week. Do not over-rely on dealer goodwill — they will not promote your brand.

13. TEST CAMPAIGNS ARE MANDATORY RISK MANAGEMENT (Ch 15). Any question in advertising can be answered cheaply and finally by a test in a few towns. A $3,000-$5,000 test replaces a $500,000 mistake. The test scale generalizes: what a thousand customers do, a million will do. Test headline variants, offer variants, sample vs no-sample, product form variants — all by actual keyed returns, never by argument. The largest advertiser Hopkins knew built 26 profitable product lines by testing one at a time. Do not scale until the test proves safety.

14. INDIVIDUALITY: MAINTAIN ONE PERSONA (Ch 17). An ad campaign develops a personality. Change it and you lose the trust built. Signed ads, named spokespeople, and consistent tone all build a recognizable character readers come to trust. Playing a different character each campaign destroys accumulated equity.

15. NEGATIVE ADVERTISING LOSES 4 TO 1 (Ch 18). Never attack rivals. Never show what you cure (the wrinkle, the bad teeth, the failure). Show only the positive outcome: beautiful face, healthy teeth, the successful man. Positive ads outpull negative ads four to one. Show what readers wish to become, not what they are trying to escape.

16. LETTER WRITING FOLLOWS SAME RULES (Ch 19). Every follow-up letter is an ad. Test letters exactly as you test ads — one against another by actual response. Strike while the iron is hot; every action-getting letter sets a time limit or creates urgency. Continue the theme that created the inquiry; do not introduce a new argument.

17. NAMING MATTERS AT FOUNDING (Ch 20). A product name that tells the benefit story (Cream of Wheat, Minute Tapioca, Holeproof) is a permanent advertising asset. A meaningless coined name (Kodak) works if owned exclusively. Descriptive generic names (Malted Milk, Toasted Corn Flakes) are the worst: you build a demand and share it with everyone.

18. KEY EVERY AD; MEASURE COST PER CUSTOMER (Ch 21). Hopkins saw major advertisers spending $700,000 per year not knowing if advertising worked at all. The only question that matters is cost per customer acquired and revenue per customer over time. Unkeyed ads are money spent blindly. Every campaign must have a mechanism to trace returns. Scientific advertising is impossible without instrumentation.

CORE OPERATING RULE SET (distilled for SNIPED use):
- Copy serves one function: make the sale. Strip everything else.
- Specificity creates belief. Vague claims create discount.
- Headlines select the right reader. Spend more time on them than on body copy.
- Test everything cheap before scaling expensive. $3k test saves $500k mistake.
- Samples and offers must be earned via expressed interest, not scattered.
- Maintain one brand persona across all touchpoints. Consistency builds accumulated trust.
- Show the positive outcome, never the problem being solved.
- Name your thing with a coined, ownable word that can typify the category.
- Research the consumer before writing a single word of copy.
- Measure cost per customer, always. No measurement = no advertising science.
contradictions: The OS leans toward premium brevity and restraint in copy; Hopkins explicitly and repeatedly proves via keyed returns that LONGER copy produces MORE sales, not less. 'The more you tell the more you sell' is not a heuristic — it is a tested empirical finding. SNIPED's premium visual restraint is a STYLE choice, not a copy-length choice. These are separable and should not be conflated.

The OS uses 'keep your name visible / brand awareness' framing in some contexts (LinkedIn presence, IG mythology). Hopkins explicitly says: 'It is not to keep your name before the people.' Awareness spend that cannot be traced to cost per customer is the primary waste Hopkins spent the book dismantling. This does not mean brand-building is wrong for SNIPED, but the OS should explicitly separate which spend is measurable conversion vs intentional brand equity, rather than treating all spend as equally valid.

Hopkins says do not attack rivals and never position negatively. The OS 'anti-AI' defense posture, if written as what we refuse to do rather than what we deliver, is structurally negative advertising. Hopkins would reframe: not 'we don't use AI on your face' but 'your likeness, untouched — the standard premium photography commands.' The positive framing of the same position.
chunk_accuracy_note: The 5 prior chunks captured the top 3 principles accurately (salesmanship axiom, test-and-trace, specificity) but missed: the mail-order-as-gold-standard framework, the psychology chapter's tested levers (pay-later beats refund, personalization, exclusivity, price-signals-quality), the named-persona/individuality doctrine, the sample distribution rules (earned not scattered), the distribution-via-coupon strategy, the costs-too-much chapter (don't try to change habits), the negative-vs-positive 4-to-1 proven result, and the naming-at-founding strategic decision. The 5th chunk ('Hormozi' synthesis) introduced content not present in the book at all — Hopkins never references Hormozi — which is a fabrication artifact, not an extraction. Coverage is 30-40 percent of the actual usable doctrine.
gate_candidates: Before writing any SNIPED copy, confirm: (1) specific claim or figure replaces every generality, (2) headline selects correct reader explicitly, (3) full story told in one exposure, (4) positive outcome shown not problem depicted, (5) offer framed as service not request-to-buy
workflow_candidates: Test-campaign protocol: run offer variant in 1-2 local markets with keyed tracking (unique URL, coupon code, or tracked link) before national/full rollout; measure cost per inquiry and cost per booked client; scale only the variant that wins
